summary: A 352-foot granite column at Put-in-Bay honoring Perry's 1813 victory on Lake Erie; the Coast Guard added navigation lights in 1940.

structures.note: 352 ft, pink Milford granite; the navigation light is on the roof of the monument (Light List 2025)

access.note: National Park Service memorial. Grounds, memorial plaza and rotunda are free. The observation deck is not accessible in the 2026 and 2027 seasons because of the Upper Plaza Rehabilitation.

events.note: 2015 nomination: a cornerstone 'set there in 1858' on Gibraltar Island; the 1966 nomination dates the Gibraltar cornerstone to 1859. The sources disagree.

1966 nomination: cornerstone laid on Gibraltar Island in 1859. 2015 nomination: the laying of the cornerstone was at the 10 September 1859 celebration (but see the 1858 entry). The 1966 nomination says the Gibraltar monument was never completed and is marked only with a bronze plaque; the 2015 nomination says Jay Cooke's 1864 monument with its bronze plaque still stands.
Architects Joseph H. Freedlander and Alexander D. Seymour selected by competition; construction began in December 1912
Cornerstone ceremonies 4 July 1913; remains of three American and three British officers reinterred beneath the rotunda floor on 11 September 1913
Memorial opened to the public on 13 June 1915
Lightning damaged the column in July 1920; the 2015 nomination says no lightning protection had been designed, and none was installed
Electric floodlights installed to light the column at night
President Roosevelt declared the memorial a national monument on 2 June 1936; a 6 July 1936 proclamation placed it in the National Park Service
Coast Guard added two marine-type navigational lights to the monument's illuminating equipment; the USLHS place record gives 1940 as the year established

Coast Guard permitted to install two navigational lights with guard rails on the penthouse; the 2015 nomination says they 'formerly provided navigational assistance' and that the current lights are much smaller
NPGallery record for NRIS 66000118 gives 15 October 1966 as the date published (the record date)
Severe storms in 1972 and 1973 destroyed most of the 1,000-foot south seawall and flooded the grounds
NPGallery record for the boundary increase (NRIS 15000185) gives 28 April 2015 as the date published
Observation deck not accessible in the 2026 and 2027 seasons because of the Upper Plaza Rehabilitation

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The USLHS place record and LighthouseFriends date the navigation light to 1940 (two marine-type lights added by the Coast Guard). The column was lit by electric floodlights from 1928, a decorative light that the 1940 bulletin says did not serve vessel traffic. The 1953 Coast Guard lights were later replaced by smaller ones. The story dates the navigation light to 1940.
The record's ENC-based values (focal height 103.9 m, range 7.8 nm) differ from the 2025 Light List (352 ft, about 107.3 m; range 9 nm). The facts use the Light List.

The 1966 nomination dates the Gibraltar cornerstone laying to 1859. The 2015 nomination places the laying at the 10 September 1859 celebration, but also refers to 'the cornerstone set there in 1858' under a monument Jay Cooke erected in 1864. The story states both dates and does not choose.

notes_for_editor: No keepers: the USLHS roster lists none and no source read names a resident keeper, so the keepers and after-keepers chapters are left out; the NPS owns the monument and the Coast Guard maintained the navigation lights (2015 nomination). The 1940 Coast Guard bulletin is cited only as quoted by LighthouseFriends; the original was not found, and no 1900-1939 Lighthouse Service report in the corpus mentions a monument light. The 2015 nomination's 1953 lights are described as 'formerly' providing navigational assistance; the current lights are smaller. The duplicate record us-oh-perrys-memorial (Wikidata stub) is already hidden and merged. Visit flag: the record says climbable true, but the NPS says the observation deck is closed in 2026 and 2027; the facts set climbable false. Third-party npplan.com says the rotunda and deck are closed until 2028; not used, since the NPS page is the authority and does not say that. The LighthouseFriends attribution of the architect as 'Freelander' is spelled Freedlander in both NRHP forms; the story uses Freedlander. Freedlander's first name is Joseph H. (1966 nomination) and Joseph Henry (2015). The 2015 nomination's 1961 construction history is Mongin's (not read directly). The monument's 1972-73 storm damage is from the continuation sheets of the 1966 nomination as revised in 1976. Second pass: the 'After the keepers' chapter is used for the post-1931 history (national monument, Coast Guard lights, 1953 lights) because the guide's chapter names are fixed and the monument has no keepers; it is not a keepers' chapter. The 1912 selection of the architects comes from the 2015 nomination's chronology row (which spells the name 'Freedman'); the 1966 nomination's competition text is quoted without a date. NPGallery 'Date Published' is the record date, not a formal listing date, so the story says so. The 1940 date is from LighthouseFriends' quotation of the Coast Guard bulletin and the USLHS place record (established 1940). The 1953 lights are described from the 2015 nomination without a height, since the height figure in the nomination is ambiguous. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the Gibraltar cornerstone paragraph now states both nominations' dates. The 2015 nomination gives the 10 September 1859 ceremony as the laying and separately says 'the cornerstone set there in 1858'; the story no longer says the 2015 nomination alone dates a stone to 1858. The architect's full name (Alexander Duncan Seymour) is cited to the 2015 nomination, not the 1966 form, which gives A. D. Seymour. LighthouseFriends spells the architect Freelander and gives the judging date 25 January 1912; the story keeps the nominations' Freedlander. The 4 July 1913 cornerstone date is in the 2015 nomination; the 1966 OCR reads 'July h'. The NPGallery dates are record dates (Date Published) and are described that way in the story.
